## Simulation College Football & Pro Football League

# Preface

This is a working document that will be a compilation of all past dev diaries and will contain up-to-date information on participating in SimSN’s SimCFB and SimNFL online leagues.

# Overview

# Steps for Signing Up

**_Need to update this section considering the links are old_**

You can find a list of all current owners and their teams on the available teams page. Any team or role with a blue “Request” button is in need of a user. Once you’ve submitted a request, an admin will review & approve as needed. Reviews can take anywhere from a few minutes to a day at most. For college, your conference commissioner will be along shortly to approve your application. For pro, you may want to reach out to the SimNFL team owner directly and ask if they are accepting staff applications.

# Strategy \- Schemes & Formations

Schemes are the blueprints on how your offense & defense behave on the football field. It’s your team’s identity and is an archetype on how the team coordinates passes, runs, and other types of plays. Schemes are stronger in some aspects of the game than others, and will also be weaker than others. There is no best scheme, nor is there a worst scheme. Each scheme comes down to a matter of preference for the user and how they want to build their team.

## Offensive Schemes

Up first is the offense. Previously, there were only four options here: Pro, Air Raid, Spread Option, and Double Wing. Now, we will expand that number by three times to 12\. We have also grouped the new offenses into three categories: Pro, Spread, and Smashmouth. You can definitely still see some resemblance to the old schemes, but there is a lot more granularity and options to choose from.

### Personnel

Before we dive in & introduce the new schemes, I want to go over the concept of personnel first, as this is a big key to how the schemes differ. In short, personnel determine who is on the field for you. Each formation has a personnel associated with it (I formation, for example, is 21 personnel: two RBs, 1 TE, and 2 WRs), and many schemes only have one formation per personnel group, so that formation is likely the only way to get that particular grouping of players on the field.

### Formation

So now that we have established personnel, now we can talk about formations. Formations are just the name that each scheme gives to the personnel group and let's you know how the players are lining up on the field. Each scheme will have 5 formations to choose from, but you will only be able to pick two or three for each game. You will be allowed to change between any of the five formations your scheme offers without penalty. However, overall scheme changes still will have scheme change penalties associated.

As I go through the formations, I will give what personnel are included on the field in that formation.

## Pro Scheme Group

This scheme group is defined by a mostly balanced approach (run vs. pass) in addition to usually having 1-2 RB, 1-2 TE and about 2-3 WR.

### Power Run

- Formations:
  - I Formation: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
  - Singleback: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Double Tight: RB1, TE1, TE2, WR1, WR2
  - I Formation Heavy: RB1, FB1, TE1, TE2, WR1
  - Split Back Gun: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
- Scheme Fits: Power RB, Blocking FB, Blocking TE, Red Zone Threat WR, Run Blocking OL
- Bad Fits: Speed RB, Receiving RB, FB and TE, Vertical Threat TE, Pass Blocking OL
- Notes: This scheme centers around using the run to set up the pass. Most run-heavy pro schemes, but still a good amount of passing will be available.

### Vertical

- Formations:
  - I Formation: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
  - Singleback: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Double Tight: RB1, TE1, TE2, WR1, WR2
  - Singleback Gun: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Spread Gun: RB1, WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4
- Scheme Fits: Pocket QB, Receiving RB, Receiving FB, Receiving and Vertical Threat TE, Route Runner and Speed WR, Pass Blocking OL
- Bad Fits: Balanced, Scrambler, and Field General QBs, Power RB, Blocking and Rushing FB, Blocking TE, Red Zone Threat WR, Run Blocking OL
- Notes: This scheme centers on the long pass, but still allows for quite a bit of running.

### West Coast

- Formations:
  - Near/Far: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
  - Singleback: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Spread: RB1, WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4
  - Singleback Gun: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Split Back Gun: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
- Scheme Fits: Field General QB, Balanced and Receiving FB, Receiving TE, Route Runner and Possession WR, Line Captain C
- Bad Fits: Blocking FB, Red Zone Threat WR
- Notes: This scheme centers on the short pass, but still allows for a bit of running.

### I Options

- Formations:
  - I Formation: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
  - Singleback: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Double Tight: RB1, TE1, TE2, WR1, WR2
  - Singleback Gun: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Split Back Gun: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
- Scheme Fits: Scrambler QB, Power RB, Rushing FB, Blocking TE, Possession WR
- Bad Fits: Pocket QB, Speed and Receiving RB, Receiving FB, Receiving and Vertical Threat TE.
- Notes: This scheme offers up the ability to run a lot more option-type plays, but still is mainly balanced in run vs. pass.

## Spread Scheme Group

This scheme group is defined by a pass-focused approach in addition to usually having 1 or fewer RB, 1 or fewer TE and several WR.

### Run and Shoot

- Formations:
  - Spread: RB1, WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4
  - Singleback: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Spread Gun: RB1, WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4
  - Singleback Gun: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Empty Gun: WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4, WR5
- Scheme Fits: Field General QB, Speed and Receiving RB, Speed WR, Line Captain C
- Bad Fits: Balanced and Power RB, Blocking and Rushing FB, Blocking TE, Possession WR
- Notes: This scheme focuses on short passes and passes far more often than it runs.

### Air Raid

- Formations:
  - Spread Gun: RB1, WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4
  - Singleback Gun: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Empty Gun: WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4, WR5
  - Big Spread Gun: RB1, TE1, TE2, WR1, WR2
  - Pony Spread Gun: RB1, RB2, WR1, WR2, WR3
- Scheme Fits: Pocket QB, Receiving RB, Receiving and Vertical Threat TE, Speed WR, Pass Blocking OL
- Bad Fits: Balanced, Scrambler, and Field General QBs, Power RB, Blocking and Rushing FB, Blocking TE, Run Blocking OL
- Notes: This scheme focuses on long passes and passes far more often than it runs.

### **Pistol**

- Formations:
  - Pistol: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Power Pistol: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
  - Heavy Power Pistol: RB1, FB1, TE1, TE2, WR1
  - Big Pistol: RB1, TE1, TE2, WR1, WR2
  - Spread Pistol: RB1, WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4
- Scheme Fits: Balanced and Pocket QB, Balanced RB, Rushing FB, Vertical Threat TE, Route Runner and Possession WR
- Bad Fits: Balanced FB, Line Captain C
- Notes: This scheme is the most balanced of the spread offenses and has limited access to option-type plays.

### Spread Option

- Formations:
  - Spread Gun: RB1, WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4
  - Singleback Gun: RB1, TE1, WR1, WR2, WR3
  - Split Back Gun: RB1, RB2, TE1, WR1, WR2
  - Big Spread Gun: RB1, TE1, TE2, WR1, WR2
  - Pony Spread Gun: RB1, RB2, WR1, WR2, WR3
- Scheme Fits: Scrambler QB, Speed RB, Receiving FB, Route Runner and Possession WR
- Bad Fits: Balanced RB, Balanced FB
- Notes: This scheme offers up the ability to run a lot more option-type plays, but focuses on pass plays still.

## Smashmouth Scheme Group

This scheme group is defined by a run-focused approach in addition to usually having 2-3 RB, 1-3 TE and very few WR.

### Wing-T

- Formations:
  - Wing-T: RB1, RB2, FB1, TE1, WR1
  - T-Split: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
  - Wing-T Double Tight: RB1, RB2, FB1, TE1, TE2
  - Split Back Gun: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
  - Wing Split Back Gun: RB1, RB2, FB1, TE1, WR1
- Scheme Fits: Balanced QB, Balanced RB, Balanced FB, Speed WR
- Bad Fits: None
- Notes: This scheme has the most balanced approach (run vs. pass) of the smashmouth scheme group.

### Double Wing

- Formations:
  - Double Wing: RB1, RB2, FB1, TE1, TE2
  - Double Wing Strong: RB1, RB2, FB1, TE1, WR1
  - Double Wing Wide: RB1, RB2, FB1, WR1, WR2
  - Double Wing Spread: FB1, WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4
  - Double Wing Split: RB1, FB1, TE1, TE2, WR1
- Scheme Fits: Power RB, Blocking and Rushing FB, Blocking TE, Red Zone Threat WR, Run Blocking OL
- Bad Fits: Pocket QB, Speed and Receiving RB, Receiving FB, Receiving and Vertical Threat TE, Pass Blocking OL
- Notes: This scheme has barely any access to pass plays.

### Wishbone

- Formations:
  - Wishbone: RB1, RB2, FB1, TE1, TE2
  - Wishbone Strong: RB1, RB2, FB1, TE1, WR1
  - Wishbone Wide: RB1, RB2, FB1, WR1, WR2
  - I Formation Heavy: RB1, FB1, TE1, TE2, WR1
  - I Formation: RB1, FB1, TE1, WR1, WR2
- Scheme Fits: Balanced and Field General QB, Balanced RB, Red Zone Threat WR
- Bad Fits: Balanced FB, Route Runner WR, Line Captain C
- Notes: This scheme is also fairly balanced (run vs. pass) like the Wing-T, but it does not have access to any shotgun formations.

### Flexbone

- Formations:
  - Flexbone: RB1, RB2, FB1, TE1, TE2
  - Flexbone Strong: RB1, RB2, FB1, TE1, WR1
  - Flexbone Wide: RB1, RB2, FB1, WR1, WR2
  - Flexbone Gun: RB1, RB2, FB1, TE1, TE2
  - Flexbone Gun Wide: RB1, RB2, FB1, WR1, WR2
- Scheme Fits: Scrambler QB, Speed RB, Balanced FB, Red Zone Threat WR
- Bad Fits: Balanced RB, Speed and Possession WR
- Notes: This scheme offers up the ability to run a lot more option-type plays, but is almost entirely run-focused.

## Defensive Schemes

Next, we have the defense. Previously the schemes were a generic 4-3 vs. a 3-4 which really weren't even schemes; they were formations. Once again, we will have three times the number of schemes with six for defense.

### Personnel

Just like offenses, defenses have personnel. Also just like on offense, personnel determine who is on the field for you. Each formation has a personnel associated with it (4-3 Base, for example with 4 DL, 3 LB and 4 DB), and many schemes only have one formation per personnel group, so that formation is likely the only way to get that particular grouping of players on the field. I will list the personnel of each formation.

### Formation

Again, formations are just the name that each scheme gives to the personnel group and lets you know how the players are lining up on the field. Defenses will have five formations to choose from, but will not be limited in the number they can field, but why that is will have to be saved for a future dev diary. You will be allowed to change between any of the five formations your scheme offers without penalty. However, overall scheme changes still will have scheme change penalties associated. When I list personnel in a formation, the two '|' characters show the separation between the DL, LB, and DB groups.

### Strengths and Weaknesses

Each defense will have two offenses that they are good against (they will get bonuses against them) and two offenses they are weak against (they get maluses). Any other offensive scheme will not have any modifiers applied. I will list these under each defensive scheme.

### Old School Front 7 Man

- Formations:
  - 4-4 Base: (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | LOLB1, MLB1, MLB2, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1)
  - 4-4 Over (LOLB1, LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | MLB1, MLB2, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1)
  - 4-4 Under (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1, ROLB1 | LOLB1,MLB1, MLB2| CB1, CB2, FS1)
  - 4-3 Light (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | LOLB1, MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1, SS1)
  - 4-2-5 Nickel (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1)
- Scheme Fits: Run Stopper OLB, Field General and Run Stopper ILB
- Bad Fits: Coverage OLB and ILB
- Strengths: Flexbone and Wishbone
- Weaknesses: Vertical and West Coast

### 2-Gap Zone

- Formations:
  - 3-4 Okie (LE1, DT1, RE1 | LOLB1, MLB1, MLB2, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1, SS1)
  - 3-4 Bronco (LE1, DT1, RE1, ROLB1 | LOLB1, MLB1, MLB2 | CB1, CB2, FS1, SS1)
  - 3-4 Eagle (LOLB1, LE1, DT1, RE1, ROLB1 | MLB1, MLB2 | CB1, CB2, FS1, SS1)
  - 3-3-5 Nickel (LE1, RE1, ROLB1 | LOLB1, MLB1, MLB2 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1)
  - 3-2-6 Dime (LE1, RE1, ROLB1 | MLB1, MLB2 | CB1, CB2, CB3, CB4, FS1, SS1)
- Scheme Fits: Run Stopper DE, Nose Tackle DT, Run Stopper and Pass Rush OLB, Run Stopper ILB
- Bad Fits: Speed Rush DE, Pass Rusher DT, Speed OLB and ILB
- Strengths: Wing-T and Double Wing
- Weaknesses: Spread Option and Pistol

### 4-man Front Spread Stopper Zone

- Formations:
  - 4-2-5 Base (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1)
  - 4-1-6 Dime (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | MLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, CB4, FS1, SS1)
  - 4-1-6 Big Dime (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | MLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1, SS2)
  - 4-3 Heavy (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | SS2, MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1, SS1)
  - 4-4 Jumbo (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | SS1. SS2, MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1)
- Scheme Fits: Speed Rush DE, Pass Rusher DT, Coverage OLB and ILB
- Bad Fits: Nose Tackle DT, Run Stopper DE, OLB, ILB
- Strengths: Air Raid and Pistol
- Weaknesses: Flexbone and Wishbone

### 3-man Front Spread Stopper Zone

- Formations:
  - 3-3-5 Base (LE1, DT1, RE1 | LOLB1, MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1)
  - 3-3-5 Over (LOLB1, LE1, DT1, RE1 | MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1)
  - 3-2-6 Big Penny (LE1, DT1, RE1 | MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1, SS2)
  - 3-2-6 Penny (LE1, DT1, RE1 | MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, CB4, FS1, SS1)
  - 3-4-4 Heavy (LE1, DT1, RE1 | SS1, LOLB1, MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1)
- Scheme Fits: Nose Tackle DT, Pass Rush OLB, Coverage ILB
- Bad Fits: Run Stopper OLB, ILB, Speed OLB and ILB, Field General ILB
- Strengths: Run and Shoot and Spread Option
- Weaknesses: Power Run and I-Option

### Speed Man

- Formations:
  - 4-3 Base (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | LOLB1, MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1, SS1)
  - 4-3 Over (LOLB1, LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1, SS1)
  - 4-2-5 Nickel (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1)
  - 4-1-6 Dime (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | MLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1, SS2)
  - 4-4 Heavy (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | SS1, LOLB1, MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1)
- Scheme Fits: Speed Rush DE, Pass Rusher DT, Coverage and Speed OLB, Speed ILB
- Bad Fits: Run Stopper DE, Nose Tackle DT, Pass Rush OLB, Field General ILB
- Strengths: Vertical and West Coast
- Weaknesses: Wing-T and Double Wing

### Multiple Man

- Formations:
  - 4-3 Base (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | LOLB1, MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1, SS1)
  - 4-3 Over (LOLB1, LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, FS1, SS1)
  - 3-4 Bronco (LE1, DT1, RE1, ROLB1 | LOLB1, MLB1, MLB2 | CB1, CB2, FS1, SS1)
  - 4-2-5 Over (LE1, DT1, RE1, ROLB1 | MLB1, MLB2 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1)
  - 4-2-5 Nickel (LE1, DT1, DT2, RE1 | MLB1, ROLB1 | CB1, CB2, CB3, FS1, SS1)
- Scheme Fits: Run Stopper DE, Speed OLB, Speed and Field General ILB
- Bad Fits: Speed Rush DE, Pass Rusher DT, Coverage OLB and ILB
- Strengths: Power Run and I-Option
- Weaknesses: Run and Shoot and Air Raid

# The NewSim Playbook — A Coach's Field Manual

_Everything a new coach needs to know about how a SimSN football game is actually played out, from the
opening coin toss to the final whistle._

Welcome to the sideline. You've got a roster, a depth chart, and a gameplan card full of dials and
sliders — but what actually happens when you hit "Sim"? This manual walks through the entire life
of a simulated game, in order, the same way the engine itself experiences it: kickoff, drive after
drive, play after play, down to the coin-flip odds and the attribute rolls that decide whether your
star running back breaks a tackle or gets stuffed at the line.

Nothing in here is guesswork — every rule, percentage, and threshold described below is pulled
directly from the simulation code. Think of this as
the manual that would ship in the box if NewSim were a physical cartridge.

## How the Game Is Built

Think of NewSim as two departments working together:

- **The Front Office** (`NewSim/` project) — this is the department that schedules games, pulls
  rosters and gameplans off the wire, and calls out "next play" until the final whistle. Its main
  files are `Run Game.cs` and `GameManagement.cs`.
- **The Field** (`NewSimResources/` project) — this is where the actual football happens. Every
  formation, every blitz, every stiff-arm is resolved here using probability tables loaded from CSV
  files under `Mapping Data/` and `NFL Mapping Data/` (via `Mappings`/`Importer`), cross-referenced
  against each player's 0–100 attribute ratings.

There's no physics engine and no field grid — NewSim is a **tabletop-style simulation**. Every play
boils down to a series of weighted dice rolls: pick a formation, pick a play, pick a matchup, roll
against a table, apply modifiers, done. This manual explains, in order, exactly which dice get
rolled and when.

## Pre-Game: Setting the Table

Before the coin even leaves the referee's hand, the engine (`RunGame.RunGamesWeb` →
`RunOneOfManyGames`) has to build both teams from scratch for this single game:

1. **Import the rulebook.** `Mappings.Import()`/`NFLImport()` loads every probability table the
   game will ever consult.
2. **Pull the schedule.** Games are grouped into timeslots (Thursday, Friday, Saturday
   morning/afternoon/evening/night for college; Thursday/Sunday-noon/Sunday-afternoon/Sunday-night/
   Monday for the pros) and run one at a time.
3. **Build both rosters.** `WebFunctions.ReturnTeam` downloads each team's roster, depth chart, and
   gameplan and turns them into a `GameTeam` — a `Player` list, a `DepthChart`, and a `Gameplan`.
   Along the way:
   - Weather adjusts stamina, catching/carrying, and kicking/throwing ratings for both sides.
   - The **away team only** gets hit with a **crowd-noise penalty** scaled by stadium size and each
     player's `Discipline` rating — this is important enough to get its own chapter (see §12).
4. **Load the playbook cards.** Each team's configured runner/receiver preferences
   (`RunnerDistributionRB1`, `TargetingWR1`, etc.) are turned into weighted lists the play-callers
   will draw from all game long.
5. **Take attendance.** `GameTeam.AddPlayers()` builds one deduplicated roster list per team, and a
   snapshot of the Week 1 starting lineup is saved (`DepthChart.SeedStarterSnapshot`) so healthy
   starters can be restored later if backups had to step in for stamina or injury reasons.
6. **Warm up the legs.** `Stamina.Seed` gives every player a starting energy tank.
7. **Flip the coin.** Two independent 50/50 rolls (`ChoiceIsHeads`, `CoinTossIsHeads`) decide the
   away team's call and the actual result; whoever wins gets the option, and the engine defaults to
   giving that team the ball to open the game.

With both teams built and the coin flipped, kickoff begins.

## Kickoff! Starting Any Half (or Any Drive After a Score)

Every kickoff in the game — the opening kick, the second-half kick, and every kick after a
touchdown or a successful field goal — runs through the exact same routine:

1. **Pick the units.** 11 players per side are pulled from the depth chart: a kicker and coverage
   unit for the kicking team, and two return men plus blockers for the receiving team.
2. **Roll for trouble.** The engine checks for a random event (injury/fumble/penalty/big-play — see
   §11) and specifically checks for a kickoff penalty.
3. **Kick it.**
   - The coverage unit's and return unit's overall ratings are built from a blend of Strength,
     Speed, Agility, Football IQ, and Tackle.
   - A base landing spot is rolled from a kick-power/accuracy table, then nudged forward or back
     based on which unit — coverage or return — is better.
   - **80% of kickoff returns** go to the depth chart's #1 return man; the other 20% go to the
     backup.
   - If the ball lands in or near the end zone, it may be a touchback — or the returner might
     occasionally take a knee even when a return was available.
   - If it's returned, a base return distance is rolled from the returner's speed/agility, then
     adjusted the same way (coverage rating vs. return rating), checked for a touchdown or an
     out-of-bounds result, and a tackler is credited.
4. **Bank the play.** Stats, play-by-play text, and stamina drain are recorded for everyone
   involved.

## Extra Point or Two-Point Try?

Every touchdown triggers a decision (`Gameplan.GoFor2`) based on the score **before** the
touchdown is added. This is a fixed strategy card, not a live "judgment call" — for example:

- Down by **8** in the second half or later → always go for 2.
- Down by **14, 9, 7, 6, 4, 3, 1**, tied, up by **2, 3**, or up by **6–11** → never go for 2, kick
  the extra point.
- Down by **12** or up by **4** late in the 4th quarter → a coin-flip-ish chance to go for 2
  (25%/50% respectively).
- In **NCAA's third overtime and beyond**, 2-point tries are mandatory — no more kicking.

Going for 2 runs one normal play from the 2-yard line. Kicking the extra point runs through
`GameManagement.RunXP`, which almost always succeeds unless the rushing team's block chance comes
through — with `FormationPopulator.IsClutchKick` flagging especially tense kicks as "clutch" (see
§10) based on score and time remaining.

## The Flow of a Quarter

The main game loop (`RunQuarter`) plays snap after snap until the clock in that quarter hits zero
(with a bonus untimed down if a defensive penalty demands it). On every snap, the engine:

1. **Checks if a kickoff is due** — if the last play was a score, restart at §3.
2. **Reads the clock.** In the final two minutes of the 2nd and 4th quarters, hurry-up/no-huddle
   behavior kicks in for a trailing offense.
3. **Makes the 4th-down call** (`Gameplan.GoForIt`) — field goal, punt, or go for it, decided by:
   - Whether the line of scrimmage is inside the team's configured field-goal range.
   - Score and time (with special-case logic for kneeling out a win and for always going for it
     when down by a field goal or less in the final two minutes).
   - Otherwise, a straight percentage roll — separate dials for "4th and short" (distance ≤ 3) and
     "4th and long," both tunable per team, with the CPU defaulting to 10% go-for-it on short and
     0% on long.
4. **Runs the play** — field goal, punt, or a normal offensive snap (run, pass, option, or RPO —
   see §7 and §8) — then updates down, distance, field position, and score. A safety ends the
   quarter immediately.

## Halftime and Overtime

At halftime, the team that didn't receive the opening kickoff now receives — a fresh kickoff plays
out exactly like §3. If the game is tied after regulation:

- **College overtime**: no punts allowed. Each team gets one untimed possession starting at the
  opponent's 25-yard line, alternating who goes first. Starting in the **third overtime period**,
  both teams are forced into 2-point-try-only plays from the 2-yard line — no more field goals or
  full drives.
- **Pro overtime**: a single continuous 10-minute period that starts with a normal kickoff and then
  plays out like sudden death — next score (with the usual exceptions) wins.

## Calling the Play: How the AI Coaches Think

### Reading the situation

Before every non-special-teams snap, the engine classifies the down/distance/clock/score into one
of seven "situations" (`PreBuiltGameplans.getSituation`):

| Situation         | Trigger                                          |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Normal            | Anything not covered below                       |
| 3rd-and-short     | 3rd down, ≤3 yards to go                         |
| 3rd-and-long      | 3rd down, >3 yards to go                         |
| 4th-and-short     | 4th down, ≤3 yards to go                         |
| 4th-and-long      | 4th down, >3 yards to go                         |
| Two-Minute Drill  | ≤4:00 left in the half, offense trailing or tied |
| Four-Minute Drill | ≤4:00 left in the half, offense ahead            |

Any 3rd/4th down or a clock under four minutes marks the moment as **clutch** (see §10). The
offense's gameplan is then temporarily reshaped for this one play only — its permanent settings are
never touched:

- Run/pass/option/RPO weights shift hard toward the situation (e.g. a Two-Minute Drill multiplies
  run weight by 0.05 and pass weight stays at 1.00; 4th-and-long zeroes out everything except pass).
- The **defense's** blitz aggression and run/pass "keying" also shift, based on a rock-paper-scissors
  matchup between the offense's scheme family (Pro-style, Spread-style, or Smashmouth-style) and the
  defense's scheme family (Blitz-Heavy, Balanced, or Cautious) — e.g. a blitz-heavy defense facing a
  smashmouth offense on 4th-and-short will blitz roughly 90% of the time.
- CPU-controlled teams always play conservative 4th-down football (10% go-for-it on short, 0% on
  long, 50-yard max field-goal range) regardless of their configured settings; human-configured
  teams keep their own dials.

### Picking a formation and personnel

The offense rolls a formation from its (up to five) configured options, weighted by how often the
coach wants to run each one, then rolls again to decide whether this snap is a **traditional run**,
**traditional pass**, **option run**, or **RPO**. The matching defensive formation and call
(run/pass tendency, blitz aggression, zone/man shells) is picked the same way, and personnel for
both sides is pulled straight from the depth chart for that formation.

### Picking the actual play

- **Run plays**: a weighted roll across the team's run-type mix (Outside/Inside Left/Right, Power
  Left/Right, Draw Left/Right), then a weighted roll to pick which back or receiver actually
  carries — receivers/tight ends barely ever touch the ball except on jet-sweep-style calls, and
  non-scrambling quarterbacks never keep it themselves.
- **Option plays**: the quarterback "reads" the defense using a formula built from his Football IQ
  against the smartest nearby defender, deciding whether to keep, hand off, or pitch.
- **RPOs**: the quarterback reads whether the defense is leaning run or pass and reacts
  accordingly — correctly reading the defense earns a small bonus; guessing wrong costs a bit of
  yardage and, on a pass, adds extra interception risk.
- **Pass plays**: a weighted roll across Short/Medium/Long/Deep/Screen/Play-Action (deep shots are
  automatically excluded once the offense is inside the opponent's 21-yard line), then a weighted
  roll to pick the target receiver based on each receiver's configured priority.
- **Focus plays**: a defensive coordinator can flag up to three specific play types they're
  "keying" on. Guess right and the defense gets a bonus; if the DC commits to exactly three focus
  calls and the offense runs something else entirely, the defense gets _punished_ for guessing
  wrong — unless that defense was on a bye the week before.

## The Snap: How a Play Actually Plays Out

### Run plays

The playbook has four base run families — **Outside Left/Right**, **Inside Left/Right**, **Power
Left/Right**, and **Draw Left/Right** — plus four option families (**Read**, **Speed**,
**Inverted**, and **Triple** Option, each Left/Right) that ultimately still resolve as an Outside or
Inside run once the ball is actually handed off, kept, or pitched. Every run assigns a ball-carrier
and a **point of attack** — a specific blocker, a specific defender, or a blocker-vs-defender
matchup pulled straight from the offensive and defensive personnel on the field (or, on a
"breakaway" call, no blocking assignment at all — straight to the long-run table). From there:

1. If there's a blitz, it's checked for success first — a skill roll across the blitzing
   defenders' IQ/speed/agility/strength. A **successful blitz** shifts a defender into an otherwise
   empty gap and costs the offense 2 yards; a **failed or non-existent blitz** hands the offense a
   free +2 yards for the defense being out of position.
2. A base "run number" is rolled (1–12), then nudged by whether the defense is keying run or pass,
   by whether an option/RPO read was correct (±1 in the pros, ±2 in college), and — for **Draw**
   plays specifically — by whether the defense bit on the fake: a draw against a defense that's
   _blitzing_ while keying run gets punished hard (the defense wasn't fooled), while a draw against
   a defense that's keying run but _holding back_ gets rewarded hard (the defense bit completely);
   a draw against a genuinely pass-committed defense gets no special treatment either way.
3. That run number indexes into one of two tables, chosen by play type, to get a base yardage:
   - **Outside runs** — and any Outside-flavored option keep or pitch — read the **Outside-Run
     table**, keyed on the ball-carrier's **Agility** and **Speed**. Anyone who isn't a running
     back takes a -5 Agility penalty for this lookup, since it's treated as an ad-lib jet sweep
     rather than a designed outside run.
   - **Inside runs, Power runs, and Draws** all share the **Inside-Run table**, keyed on the
     ball-carrier's **Strength** and **Speed** instead. Power doesn't get a separate yardage table
     of its own, but it does aim at a different, more interior point-of-attack than a plain Inside
     call, so it tends to draw a different blocker-vs-defender matchup.
4. The point-of-attack matchup then adds or subtracts yardage: the blocker's Run Blocking rating,
   the defender's (or defenders') Run Defense rating (itself a blend of Run Defense, Strength,
   Speed, and Football IQ), or a fully combined blocker-vs-defender net — a strongly winning
   blocker can even register a **pancake**.
5. Very bad runs are capped (rarely allowed to be worse than -6 yards) and mildly bad runs get a
   chance to "fight forward" for a few extra yards after contact.
6. Finally, a random event (§11) may add an injury, fumble, penalty, or a yardage multiplier.

Any option pitch or keep is still resolved as either an Outside or Inside run under the hood once
the ball-carrier is decided — the option "flavor" (Read/Speed/Inverted/Triple) only changes who
ends up holding the ball and which of the two tables above gets used.

### Pass plays

Passing is the most involved part of the whole engine. The five pass families — **Short**,
**Medium**, **Long**, **Deep**, and **Screen** — and **Play Action** (which can be tacked onto a
Medium, Long, or Deep call) each read different attributes:

1. The quarterback's throw power, accuracy, football IQ, and archetype set base
   completion/incompletion/interception ranges — and each pass type (Short/Medium/Long/Deep) has
   its own base range table and its own archetype adjustment, so the same quarterback can be far
   more comfortable on one type of throw than another.
2. The intended receiver's attributes are added on top, and **which** attributes matter changes by
   route depth:
   - **Short** routes lean on **Route Running** and **Speed**.
   - **Medium** routes lean on **Route Running** and **Agility**.
   - **Long** and **Deep** routes both lean on **Route Running** and **Speed**.
   - Every route also adds the receiver's **Catching** and **Football IQ**, and a tight end or a
     "Red Zone Threat" archetype receiver gets a small bonus once the offense is inside the 21 —
     they're simply harder to keep out of the end zone.
   - Whoever is covering the target then subtracts from all of this (zone or man, based on that
     unit's coverage rating) — an entirely open receiver gets a flat bonus instead.
3. **How the call matches up against the defense's tendency** matters a lot, and it isn't the same
   penalty for every pass type: a **Short** pass against a defense sitting on pass takes a much
   bigger completion-range hit than it does against a defense keying run (and that gap widens even
   further in the red zone), while **Medium/Long/Deep** shots are comparatively more exposed
   against a run-committed defense and comparatively safer (though still tougher) against a
   pass-committed one. **Screens** ignore this matchup penalty entirely.
4. **Play Action** stacks its own swing on top of whichever base modifier applies: it makes the
   play noticeably _easier_ to complete if the defense guessed run (they bit on the fake), and
   noticeably _harder_ if the defense guessed pass (nobody was fooled) — on top of also making it
   less likely the quarterback can bail out to a hot read if the pass rush gets home, since he's
   busy selling a fake handoff.
5. If the defense is doubling the target, coverage swings hard against the offense; if a deep shot
   targets someone _other_ than the doubled man, everyone else gets a bit easier to throw to.
6. Pass protection is worked out lineman-by-lineman against every rusher; if the pass rush actually
   gets home, the quarterback may find a "hot" receiver to bail out to instead of the original read
   (better with a high-IQ, disciplined, Field General/Pocket-passer type quarterback) — or eat a
   sack if no hot read is available.
7. A single roll then decides completion, incompletion, or interception (including a rarer
   "tipped/jumped" pick by a different defender entirely). On a completion, yardage is rolled fresh
   from a type-specific table: **Short and Medium** completions roll off the receiver's
   **Agility**, while **Long and Deep** completions roll off the receiver's **Speed** instead.
8. **Screens** skip all of the above and use their own simplified outcome table (Complete /
   Complete-and-a-half / Double / Triple / Incomplete / Pick) built around the running back's own
   carry yardage, multiplied up to roughly 1.8–1.9× once the screen connects — always targeting the
   first available back rather than a downfield receiver.
9. **Sacks** scale with how much the pass rush is winning versus the protection, translated into a
   "pressure severity" that also makes every kind of pass (especially deep shots) harder to
   complete.
10. As with run plays, a random event may still occur afterward (§11).

## Special Teams

- **Punts** work like a kickoff with an extra step up front: the return team's rush can flat-out
  block the kick before anything else happens. If it isn't blocked, distance is rolled from the
  punter's power/accuracy, with a chance to "pin" the opponent inside the 20/10/5 instead of a
  touchback (better punters pin more often), then resolved as a return exactly like a kickoff.
- **Field goals** roll a make/block chance from the kicker's power, accuracy, and the distance of
  the kick — beyond the kicker's practical range, it's an automatic miss. Good pass protection
  versus a strong rush swings the block chance; a blocked kick recovered behind the kicking team's
  own goal line is a safety.
- **Extra points** use the same math as field goals at a fixed short distance, with clutch-kick
  logic (see §10) boosting the kicker in high-pressure moments.

## Big Moments: Clutch, Focus Plays, and Scheme Matchups

- **Clutch** — 3rd/4th downs, kicks, and the final four minutes of a half all count as "clutch"
  moments. Clutch/choker personality players get their ratings temporarily boosted or nerfed during
  these plays; in the postseason, every play in the game gets this treatment.
- **Focus plays** — see §7; a correctly-guessed focus play boosts the defense, an all-wrong guess
  (with exactly three focus calls configured) can actively hurt them, unless they were on a bye the
  week before.
- **Scheme matchups** — every offensive scheme has natural advantages and disadvantages against
  certain defensive schemes (a fixed rock-paper-scissors chart across 12 offensive and 6 defensive
  schemes), applying a small attribute swing to defenders once at kickoff. A team that just switched
  schemes also suffers a temporary "still learning it" penalty (up to 25% off most attributes) that
  fades out over several weeks.

## When Things Go Wrong (or Very Right): Injuries, Fumbles, Penalties, Multipliers

After nearly every play, the engine rolls to see if something extra happens — roughly a **1-in-8
chance** per snap. If something does happen, it's one of:

- **Injury** (~38% of events, itself gated behind a further 1-in-10 roll, and skipped outright if
  more than two players are already hurt) — a random participant is selected (weighted toward the
  ball-carrier and the interior linemen), duration is rolled against that player's Injury rating
  (tougher players roll shorter injuries far more often), and the specific injury is flavor-text
  narrated based on position and severity tier (Minor/Moderate/Severe/Season-Ending).
- **Fumble** (~17%) — chance is set by the ball-carrier's Carrying rating and boosted by the
  tackler's Tackle rating; recovery is a straight 50/50 coin flip between the two teams.
- **Penalty** (~42%) — see §12 for the full discipline-driven breakdown.
- **Yardage multiplier** (~6%) — the play's result is simply doubled or tripled.

## Discipline: The Hidden Attribute That Shapes Everything

`Discipline` doesn't show up in a highlight reel, but it quietly shapes two very different parts of
the game: **how often your team gets flagged**, and **how badly your team plays away from home**.

### Discipline and penalties

Every offensive or defensive play rolls for a possible penalty (`Event.PenaltyCheck`). The process
is a two-stage roll:

1. **Which side?** The engine first flips a weighted coin for offense-vs-defense (roughly 57–60%
   offense-leaning depending on play type).
2. **Does it actually happen?** That side's chance of actually drawing a flag is driven by the
   _combined_ Discipline of all 11 players on the field (`Event.PenaltyRange`, which sums the whole
   unit's Discipline and maps it through a lookup table) — a unit full of low-discipline players is
   simply going to see more flags over the course of a game.
3. **Who's guilty?** If a penalty is confirmed, the actual culprit is picked from the eligible
   players on that unit, weighted so that **less disciplined players are far more likely to be the
   one who gets flagged** (`Penalty.GuiltyPlayer` weights each candidate by `2 × (100 − discipline)`,
   so a player with 30 Discipline is roughly 7× more likely to draw the flag than a player with 90).

In short: a disciplined roster doesn't just "look" clean — it mathematically draws fewer flags, and
when a flag _does_ happen, it's far more likely to land on your one undisciplined bad apple than
your steady veterans.

### Discipline on the road (and why stadium size matters)

Separately from penalties, Discipline also determines how well a player holds up to a hostile
road crowd. This is applied once, at roster-build time, **only to the away team**, and **never** in
a game played at a neutral site (`WebFunctions.ReturnTeam` / `Importer.ImportAwayPlayers`,
`Importer.CapacityMaxDebuff`).

Here's how it works, step by step:

1. **Discipline sets a "worst case" penalty** for that player, on a sliding scale:
   - **Discipline 17 or below** → the worst possible penalty, a flat **-7** to nearly every rating.
   - **Discipline 71 or above** → **no penalty at all** — a highly disciplined player is simply
     immune to crowd noise, no matter how big the building is.
   - **Discipline 18–70** → a smooth logarithmic curve between those two extremes (roughly -6 at 20
     discipline, -4 at 30, -2 at 50, and fading to 0 as it approaches 71).
2. **Stadium size sets its own "worst case" penalty**, based purely on capacity
   (`CapacityMaxDebuff(capacity) = round((5000 − capacity) / 10000)`):
   - Small stadiums (roughly 15,000 seats or fewer) round to **0** — a quiet crowd simply can't
     rattle anyone.
   - Mid-size stadiums land around **-2 to -4** (roughly 25,000–65,000 seats).
   - Massive stadiums (six-figure capacity) can reach **-9 or -10**.
3. **The two are compared, and the _less severe_ one wins.** The final penalty is whichever number
   is closer to zero out of the discipline-based value and the stadium-based value — **not** the
   two stacked together. That means:
   - A **highly disciplined player is immune to crowd noise even in the largest stadium**, because
     their discipline-based penalty is already 0.
   - A **team playing in a small, quiet stadium won't be rattled even if their players are
     undisciplined**, because the stadium's cap overrides the harsher discipline penalty.
   - The single worst possible outcome — the full **-7** — only happens when a genuinely
     undisciplined player (≤17 Discipline) walks into a genuinely enormous, loud road environment.
4. **The actual penalty applied is random, not fixed** — it's rolled uniformly between that worst
   case and zero (e.g. a worst case of -7 might land anywhere from 0 to -7 on any given game), so
   even the most rattled road team won't be _guaranteed_ their worst outing every single week.
5. **The penalty is broad** — it's subtracted from nearly every rating the player has (Speed,
   Agility, Carrying, Catching, Coverage, Football IQ, Blocking, Pass Rush, Throwing, Kicking, and
   more), all floored at a minimum of 1 so no stat can go negative.

**The takeaway for a coach:** road environments punish undisciplined rosters far more than
disciplined ones, and the effect scales directly with the size of the building you're walking into.
Recruiting or developing high-Discipline players pays off twice — fewer flags on any given Saturday
or Sunday, and a team that travels well no matter how loud the opposing crowd gets.

## Legs Get Tired: Stamina and Fatigue

Every player starts the game with a stamina "tank," seeded from their base Stamina rating (and
nudged by weather — hot, humid conditions drain players faster). After every single play, the
engine drains stamina from whoever was actually on the field for that snap and lets everyone else
recover a little. Fatigued or injured starters get temporarily swapped out for backups pulled from
position-specific depth pools (quarterbacks, offensive skill players, offensive line, defensive
line, linebackers, defensive backs), and once a player has rested or healed enough, the engine
restores the game's original Week-1 starting lineup rather than leaving a backup entrenched
forever.

## The Locker Room: Player Attributes at a Glance

Every player on your roster is a bundle of 0–100 ratings. Here's what each one actually controls
on the field:

| Attribute                                                              | What it does                                                                                                                                        |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Football IQ                                                            | Reading option/RPO plays as a QB, run-defense rating, recognizing blitzes and hot routes                                                            |
| Speed                                                                  | Run/pass yardage, kick/punt/interception returns, run defense                                                                                       |
| Carrying                                                               | How often a ball-carrier fumbles                                                                                                                    |
| Agility                                                                | Outside-run yardage (runners other than RBs take a penalty here), how open a receiver gets                                                          |
| Catching                                                               | A defender's interception chance, a receiver's catch/yardage odds                                                                                   |
| Route Running                                                          | A receiver's odds of getting open and completing the pass                                                                                           |
| Zone / Man Coverage                                                    | How tightly a defender covers the intended receiver, split by coverage shell                                                                        |
| Strength                                                               | Inside-run yardage, run defense, pass-block/pass-rush matchups                                                                                      |
| Tackle                                                                 | How likely a defender is to force a fumble                                                                                                          |
| Pass Block / Run Block                                                 | Offensive line performance in protection and in the run game                                                                                        |
| Pass Rush                                                              | A defender's ability to beat blockers and pressure the QB                                                                                           |
| Run Defense                                                            | How much yardage a defender takes away at the point of attack                                                                                       |
| Throw Power / Accuracy                                                 | A QB's completion and interception ranges                                                                                                           |
| Kick Power / Accuracy                                                  | Kickoff distance, field-goal make/block odds                                                                                                        |
| Punt Power / Accuracy                                                  | Punt distance, pin-vs-touchback odds                                                                                                                |
| Injury                                                                 | How quickly (and how mildly) a player recovers from getting hurt                                                                                    |
| Stamina                                                                | How big a player's in-game energy tank is                                                                                                           |
| **Discipline**                                                         | **Penalty chance and severity of the road/crowd-noise debuff — see §12**                                                                            |
| Shotgun                                                                | Formation/personnel context (under-center vs. shotgun)                                                                                              |
| Clutch                                                                 | Boosts (or, for "chokers," hurts) performance in high-pressure moments                                                                              |
| Archetype (Type/Secondary Type)                                        | Unlocks special behavior — Scramblers can keep the ball on option plays, Field Generals and Pocket passers get better hot-read instincts, and so on |
| Position / Secondary Position                                          | Where a player slots into the depth chart and which matchups they're eligible for                                                                   |
| Progression, Potential, Recruiting, Academics, Personality, Work Ethic | Off-field/career-mode traits — these don't affect play-by-play resolution during a live game                                                        |

## The Front Office: Teams, Depth Charts, and Rosters

- **`GameTeam`** is the folder that holds everything about one side for one game: identity and
  colors, whether the coach is CPU-controlled, that team's `Gameplan`, its `DepthChart`, its
  `Roster`, and a flattened, duplicate-free list of every player who could possibly take the field.
- **`DepthChart`** is the actual lineup card — starters slotted into named positions (`QB1`, `WR2`,
  `CB1`, and so on) for offense, defense, and every special-teams unit, plus six ordered "next man
  up" pools for injuries and fatigue. A saved snapshot of the opening lineup lets healthy starters
  reclaim their spot once they've recovered.
- **`Roster`** is simply the full player pool a team is allowed to carry — capped at 90 (NFL
  pre-cutdown), 63 (NFL in-season), or 99 (college) players.

# SimCFB Features & Rules

## Scheduling

For the 2027 season and onward, the interface will be used to handle scheduling out of conference games, spring game matchups, and NFL preseason games.

We have also in addition created a conference scheduler within the Interface API. This scheduler will run as part of the offseason jobs when migrating to the new season; and will ensure that all conference games are scheduled & ready as soon as the offseason begins. This will also give teams ample time in scheduling out games as needed and provides one-stop-shop for requesting & scheduling games with other opponents.

### Annual Rivalry Games

Some matchups are considered traditional, whether they’re in conference or out of conference. We currently keep a spreadsheet updated ([SimCFB Protected Rivalries](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1-AW_MCxuurZ0wqo5et81pFfoyY5IbS3HG2xtuIGPKd0/edit?usp=sharing)) on which rivalries will always be annual, and which ones will always happen during X or Y week.

If you wish for the annual games list to be adjusted, whether it’s to add a game or remove a game from the annual listing, please reach out to an Admin.

## Scheduling Criteria

Read below the criteria for using the Interface’s scheduling system.

### SimCFB Out of Conference Scheduling

Here are the basic rules:

- Each team needs exactly 12 regular season games. We’re not following the Hawai’i rule. Fly your team there at your own risk.
- A SimCFB team cannot schedule a conference opponent in an OOC matchup.
- Additionally, a SimCFB team cannot schedule an opponent that is already on their schedule.
- Teams may have up to 7 home games per regular season; but it is suggested to stay balanced at 6 home games when possible. The number of schedulable OOC games at home depends on the team’s conference schedule that is generated.
- FBS teams may only schedule up to one FCS team in their out of conference schedule. In return, FCS teams may only schedule up to one FBS team within their schedule.
- Teams may choose to have games scheduled at a neutral site should they choose to.
- The following table details how many out of conference games each team will need to schedule based on their conference affiliation.

| Conference                   | Number | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| :--------------------------- | :----- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Independents                 | 12     | Notre Dame has six rivalries scheduled automatically (Michigan, USC, Stanford, Boston College, Michigan State). The coach for Notre Dame has flexibility in making the rest of their schedule. Based on IRL policies with the ACC, Notre Dame is encouraged to schedule at least 4 ACC opponents, but they may also choose to schedule whoever they wish. At the moment because Stanford and Boston College are annual rivals, Notre Dame would only need to add two more ACC teams to their schedule, should they choose to. |

So, yeah, they need to schedule 7 out of conference opponents. ### SimCFB Spring Game Scheduling

Any SimCFB team can schedule any opponent up to once in the Spring games. Teams may have from 0 to 3 games scheduled for Spring Games. Spring Games do not count towards the actual season, but may be used to test strategies as a way to prepare for the regular season. Schedule wisely.

### SimNFL Preseason Scheduling

SimNFL teams may schedule opponents they are not facing in the regular season within the preseason. Each SimNFL team is expected to have at least one home game and one away game, with up to 3 preseason games scheduled. Additionally, SimNFL teams are expected to play starters for at least one of their games. Please coordinate with your preseason opponents on whether you intend to start starters or bench players.

Snaps attained from SimNFL preseason games do count towards progression as well.

### Can CFB Teams schedule games ahead in future seasons?

Not at this time, but it is something we may consider for the future.

## Recruiting

Every year the sim generates thousands of high school seniors, and users compete to get these new stars to sign with their program. The Recruiting Overview on the interface shows the names and positions of all these “croots”, along with a Star rating from 1-5, an Overall grade, a Potential grade, and their residing location (city, state, country). You can use the filters at the top to focus on certain positions, certain star levels, etc. If you see a player you’re interested in, click the green plus sign and he will be added to your recruiting board. No one can see your board except you.

A note on grades: “Overall” is the recruit’s current ability, while “Potential” represents the growth rate that a recruit will improve _to their current state_ over time. A player with A Potential will progress faster, but that doesn’t mean they are destined to become an “A” Overall player. Similarly, a B overall player with C- Potential isn’t “overperforming”, but simply will improve slower than average.

Recruiting takes place over 20 weeks of the regular season (real time). Every week a team gets 100 points to assign to recruits they are interested in; you can place anywhere from 1-20 points on a single player, and you can place points on as many players as you want. You must use whole numbers. You also have a number of scholarships you can offer; a player **must** get a scholarship offer from you to sign with your team. Scholarship offers are public knowledge (in the News section of the Interface, it will say a player has “received an offer” from that school), but points are hidden. _You can revoke a scholarship at any time, but you will not have the option to re-offer one to the same recruit; he will never sign with you once you’ve revoked his scholarship._

## Old Recruiting System (Affinity System)

The current recruiting system is what we call the affinity system. Each team can have 0 to many **affinities** that are endearing qualities of a school that make it an enticing place for a recruit to play at. Below is the current list of affinities:

- Academics Affinity: The school has top rated academics. Bookworms apply.
- Frontrunner Affinity: The school is considered competitive and was actively a conference champion or a playoff participant. This is one of the few dynamic affinities that we currently have.
- Large Crowds Affinity: The school has a fantastic home game environment with at least 70k fans in attendance.
- Religion Affinity: This school is religiously affiliated
- Service Affinity: This school is considered a military academy and is a place where players can go should they want to serve their country at some point (given they don’t make it to the pro league)
- Small School Affinity: The school is considered a small school meaning less than 10k undergrads in attendance.
- Small Town Affinity: The school is located in what we would consider College Town USA. Nothing to do but go to school and hit up the hole in the wall bar.
- Big City Affinity: The school is located in a large city with plenty to do.
- Media Spotlight Affinity: The school often has the limelight on them through written articles and media. This is one of the few dynamic affinities based on user participation.
- Rising Stars Affinity: The school brought in a great recruiting class and so recruits are interested in the long term on where the program is heading. This is one of the few dynamic affinities that can change based on recruiting ranking.

Currently, recruits may have 0 to 2 affinities that they may prefer, including a dynamic **Close to Home** affinity that is based on the geographic location of where they and the school are based. For each matching affinity, a team can get a 10% boost towards any points applied to a recruit. This makes it up to a 20% boost.

### RES System

The **Recruiting Efficiency Score (RES) System** is a system which dynamically changes week by week and is considered to be how a team’s points hold when recruiting a recruit at any given time. The RES system is designed to weigh in how a team performs during the season & in the long term as a way of defining prestige among teams. The top teams will have a prestige at or above 94%, most teams will be between 88 and 92%, and the worst performing teams will be 87% or below with a floor of 80%. FCS teams have their floor lowered by 20% automatically to define the difference between recruiting an FBS vs an FCS school.

The value of the modifier in the Recruiting Efficiency Score is between \-20% and 20%, meaning that the worst possible fit for a recruit is at 80% strength compared to the median school. It also means that the best possible situation has effectively 120% strength in recruiting. When pitting the best fit against the worst fit, it would be a 50% advantage for the best fit school. That's far more modest than the previous affinity system.

The nuts and bolts of how the affinity score is calculated are below, but broad strokes are this: wins and losses account for 30% of the score, postseason participation of various kinds and strengths (bowl game, conference championship appearance, conference title, playoff, etc.) account of 10%, and 50% of the score is evaluated by matching affinities.

The specific weights for the current calculations of the RES are as follows:

| Item                                                                                   | Weights |
| :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------ |
| Previous Season Overall Record Wins over Conference Games Played                       | 5.00%   |
| Previous Season Conference Wins over Conference Games Played                           | 5.00%   |
| Current Season Overall Record W over Games Played                                      | 10.00%  |
| Current Season Conference W over Games Played                                          | 10.00%  |
| Coach Career Record Wins (avg wins per season over total games per season)             | 10.00%  |
| Affinity Match 1                                                                       | 25.00%  |
| Affinity Match 2                                                                       | 25.00%  |
| Postseason Games (Full Credit for Bowl Game Participation, Bowl Outcome has No Weight) | 5.00%   |
| Conference Championship (Full Credit for Title, Half Credit for Participation)         | 5.00%   |
| Rivalry Trophies Held / Other Flavors (WIP, may be added for 2023\)                    | 0.00%   |

#### Examples

Tulsa had a perfect season last year. They maxed out every category in the RES that a school can control. Their score for the year was 100%.

If they're recruiting a player they have 1 affinity match for, their RES goes to 110%, and 120% if they match both affinities.

Because this is a modifier on the Recruiting Time Points, Tulsa's RES for a 1 affinity match recruit would be:

Week 1: (5 RTP Points in Week 1\) \* RES of 110% \= 5.5 Points logged into the recruit in week 1\.

Let's say Tulsa loses their opener. That would impact their score (0/0 games played is full credit in the RES, but once a game is played it references that outcome. 0/0=1 is meant to be an approximation of hope springing eternal in the offseason.) This would drop their baseline RES score from 100% to 94.76%. The affinity bonus still applies, so in week 2 their RES would be 104.76%.

Week 2: (5 RTP Points in Week 1 \+ 5 RTP Points in Week 2\) \* RES of 104.76% \= 10.476 Points logged into the recruit week 2\.

Oh no, they also lost their home conference opener as well\! But, to make up for that, they're spending 10 RTP points this week on the recruit instead of 5\. Their baseline RES drops to 89.56% because they're now getting 0 credit for the current season conference record.

Week 3: (5 RTP Points in Week 1 \+ 5 RTP Points in Week 2 \+ 10 RTP Points in Week 3\) \* RES of 99.56% \= 19.912 Points logged into the recruit week 2\.

Let's now say that Texas Tech has an interest in that same player and also has an affinity match, but where Tulsa had the best season, Texas Tech has the worst. For comparison of the system, let's say they start off white hot and win their first game and conference opener.

Their initial RES is 90% and they have 1 affinity match for an RES with this recruit of 100%. Let's say they win a noncon week 1 and a conference game week 2 and go into week 3 sensing a battle with Tulsa and also put in 10 puts in week 3\. This is how it would break down:

Week 1: (5 RTP Points in Week 1\) \* RES of 100% \= 5 Points logged into the recruit in week 1\.

Week 2: (5 RTP Points in Week 1 \+ 5 RTP Points in Week 2\) \* RES of 100.29% \= 10.0029 Points logged into the recruit week 2\.

Week 3: (5 RTP Points in Week 1 \+ 5 RTP Points in Week 2 \+ 10 RTP Points in Week 3\) \* RES of 100.53% \= 20.106 Points logged into the recruit week 2\.

So we can see that Texas Tech started the season at a 10% disadvantage, but in just 3 weeks were able to shorten the gap in RES score, by virtue

In a third example, let's say Texas Tech has all the plans in the world to contest this recruit, but instead of opening white hot, they fall flat on their face while Tulsa continues on pace.

Tulsa by Week 3: Baseline RES of 100% \+ 10% Affinity Bonus \= 110% \* 20 \= 22 points logged.  
Tech by Week 3: Baseline RES of 80% \+ 10% Affinity Bonus \= 90% \* 20 \= 18 points logged.

In a fourth example, let's say everything about the previous example stays the same, except Tulsa has no affinity match with this particular recruit.

Tulsa by Week 3: Baseline RES of 100% \+ 10% Affinity Bonus \= 100% \* 20 \= 20 points logged.  
Tech by Week 3: Baseline RES of 80% \+ 10% Affinity Bonus \= 90% \* 20 \= 18 points logged.

#### Takeaways from RES

The example above uses the best and worst team possible by on-field performance. Tulsa currently has the highest possible score, and Texas Tech has the lowest possible score. For most teams, their baseline RES scores are going to revolve around 90-95% throughout the season. While that's not nothing, it isn't a huge difference in impact on the total race for a recruit.

However, cumulatively, a bad season is about a 10-15% difference in RES and it takes roughly 1 affinity match to counteract that deficit. This has the intended goal of making teams that should have no business in real life of competing for recruits against powerhouse programs think twice before chasing after 5\* players \- yet at the same time doesn't completely eliminate the possibility they could get one.

Conference championships and bowl games last until the next round of games, so they can act as a buoy for teams that have a bad follow-up year. This advantage doesn't seem unrealistic, as the 'glow' doesn't come off a team in less than a year.

The longer the sim goes, the more stable a coaching record value is going to be. This should act as a stabilizing force for many programs with long-tenured programs, and will also protect coaches who take over struggling teams from being tied behind the recruiting anchor of their new team's previous season record. A 9-3 good coach taking over a 3-9 program equals out to the same credit as a 6-6 team with a 6-6 coach.

## Current Recruiting System (Profile System)

Based on the reception of the Profile System from our SimHockey simulation, we are introducing the Profile System to the SimCFB simulation.

The **Profile System** is a system that reflects the current state of a college athletic program in recruiting based on intangible and tangible attributes, while providing a numeric value in what a recruit may prefer for their college career. It is a prestige system designed to reward successful programs while giving other programs the chance to build based on both static attributes and the success of the conference.

Each college football team will have a set of nine attributes that are associated with the program's tangible and intangible attributes based on the quality of the school and the school’s facilities. Each attribute is rated between 1 and 10; 1 being the worst, 10 being the best rating.

Some attributes are dynamic; meaning that they will change every offseason based on team performance and graduating players. The remaining attributes are static due to them being qualities of the school that is being represented within the SimCFB league. These values will only change depending on if the school makes a change or an impact that correlates to one of the below attributes.

Each school will offer a different experience when recruiting with some schools being much easier to sign players with than others. For example, Tennessee, Alabama, Texas, and Ohio State are powerhouse schools that will likely be the easiest to recruit for; whereas schools such as Miami (OH), Oregon State, Jacksonville State, and UTEP may have a more difficult time building their roster.

### Program Development

**Program Development** correlates to the team’s performance across the entire legacy of the sim. Meaning, depending on how the team teams from season to season, the team’s Program Development will dynamically change in each offseason.

With the introduction of the new system, each team’s Program Development attribute will be set to 5\.

### Professional Development

**Professional Development** correlates to how often players on the team are drafted into the SimNFL. The more players are drafted into the league, the higher the bonus acquired from Professional Development.

At the start of the inaugural season, each team’s Professional Development attribute will be set to 5\.

### Traditions

**Traditions** is a reflection of the team’s overall record within the sim. This is across all coaches and covers all historical wins.

### Facilities

The **Facilities** attribute reflects the age of the IRL football program of the school but also on how up to date a program’s stadium, practice facilities, and locker room are. Newer facilities in the IRL program will give the SimCFB team a higher rating.

Facilities will be treated as a static value.

### Atmosphere

**Atmosphere** ties into the school’s home record over a four-season span. If a school has played for less than four seasons they will only count all games played thus far.

### Academic Prestige

**Academic Prestige** is rating based on how well the school does academically IRL as both a school and the athletic program.

Given that a number of schools participating in SimCFB are very acclaimed universities, the Academic Prestige rating had to be balanced with a near-even amount of teams making up each possible rating when applicable.

### College Life

**College Life** is a rating based on how well the life on campus is like at the university IRL. Some players will have preferences on whether they want to be at a school with a great social scene (party school), or if they want to play somewhere where it’s more focused on the academics or athletics program. College life is considered a static value because it’s comparative towards the IRL location and college life of the school.

### Coach Rating

**Coach rating** is a Dynamic attribute that correlates to the coach’s overall success in the sim. This variable will fluctuate at a slightly faster rate than program momentum and will equate to the coach’s success throughout their career within the sim.

New coaches entering the league will always have a CoachRating of 5\. Once the season ends, their W/L record through the season will be applied and will generate a new rating.

### Conference Prestige

**Conference Prestige** is a dynamic attribute that correlates to the level of play that’s involved in the team’s conference. Recruits will have some bias regarding the conference they would like to play in, depending on how competitive the conference is.

For the inaugural implementation, each team’s Conference Rating is 5\. At the end of every season, each team’s conference rating will be adjusted based on the post-season performance of the conference members.

### Season Momentum

**Season Momentum** is a dynamic attribute that correlates to how well the team performed the previous season. Like Coach Rating, Season Momentum follows a similar practice but will instead only intake the W/L record of the previous season. In addition, if a team wins any big games such as a rivalry game or a playoff game, the score will adjust.

### Media Spotlight

**Media Spotlight** is an interesting case where this is a dynamic attribute based on the amount of media a team posts during a season. At the moment I’m going to consider the following: 1 point per post of media content, with a maximum of 10 points.

### Truly Static Attributes

For college football, we keep track of qualities that make a school unique from the others. This includes qualities such as whether the school is religious, is a service academy, and even the geographic base of where a school is located (college town, big city). We want to keep these qualities towards these schools; however, some things are going to be hard to track or consider. Two religious schools can’t be weighed on which one is more religious than the other, which is why we’re going to count them towards being a **true** or **false** case.

### Dynamic Adjustments to Attributes

Program Development and Professional Development at the moment are the only variables that will be dynamic from season to season.

Program Development reflects the team’s on-ice success, and professional development reflects the team’s success in their players being drafted into the professional league.

If a team goes winless in the regular season, their **program development** will decrease by 2 points.

If a team wins less than 25% of their total games in the regular season, their **program development** will decrease by 2 points.

If a team wins less than 50% of their total games in the regular season, their **program development** will decrease by 1 point.

If a team wins 75% of their regular season games, their **program development** increases by 1 point.

If a team goes undefeated in the regular season, their **program development** increases by 2 points.

If a team makes it to at least the College Football Playoffs, their **program development** increases by 1 (non-stacking).

If a team makes it to the Semifinals or is the runner-up, their **program development** increases by 2 (non-stacking).

The team that wins the national championship will have their **program development** increase by 3 (non-stacking).

A team that does not have any players drafted for more than one season will have their **professional development** decrease by 1\.

A team that has at least a player drafted in consecutive seasons will have their **professional development** increase by 1\.

A team that has at least 3 players drafted in consecutive seasons will have their **professional development** increase by 2\.

If a conference does not make it to the postseason, their **conference prestige** will decrease by 1\.

If a team makes it to the Semifinals or wins the national championship, their **conference prestige** will increase by 1\.

## Player Preferences

In the same way that each team has varying attributes, players will have their preference attributes that correlate to a team’s specific attribute. Preference attributes can range between 1 and 9; 1 being the lowest, 9 being the highest.

The player preference feature is in place instead of affinities to showcase the player’s preference regarding which kind of school they would like to play for.

Player preferences generated on each recruit will be on a normalized scale, with 5 being the expected average, with a standard deviation of 2\.

## Recruiting Points Formula

SimCFB uses team profile attributes and player preferences as part of a formula determining how impactful a team’s recruiting points are on a recruit.

The following formula compares each Team Attribute with the corresponding Player Preference attribute and forms an average using each attribute applicable. At the end of the formula, if the player is either close to home or is part of a pipeline, a small bonus is added onto the end of the modifier.

The first stage of the formula sets up a base modifier using the team attribute as a weight:  
![][image1]

The second stage of the formula calculates the adjusted modifier based on the difference between the team’s attribute, and the player’s preference. The greater the difference between the team attribute and the player preference, the more impactful the modifier. The higher the player preference, the less impactful the modifier becomes.

![][image2]

And the final multiplier is calculated by the following:  
![][image3]

If the recruit is close to home to the school, a 20% (0.20pt) bonus is applied onto the modifier.

I’m going to showcase two examples on how the modifiers will work given a point submission of 10 points.

### Example 1

Michigan is recruiting Test Testaverde, a Center located in Michigan right outside Ann Arbor, MI. Below are Michigan’s team attributes and Test Testaverde’s player attributes

Michigan’s biggest strengths are in its Traditions as a program and for having one of the premier arenas in NCAA College Football. Because of that, Michigan’s Traditions, Facilities, and Atmosphere attributes are the most impactful attributes as part of the formula.

The average of all of the modifiers becomes 1.4533. Because Testaverde is considered a recruit that’s close to home, a 20% bonus is applied, making the modifier 1.4533

![][image4]

### Example 2

St. Thomas is a fairly new FCS program and is attempting to make waves in recruiting. They are attempting to recruit Seamus O’Conner, a QB based in Texas. Here is how the calculation goes:

![][image5]

Because St. Thomas’s football team is just starting, they have fairly new facilities but don’t have the same traditions that many atlantic schools have. Because Seamus deeply cares about playing at a school that offers a fantastic gameday experience – rowdy fans, large stadium, his name on the jumbotron; in addition, a program being in a historic conference led by a coach who knows how to win; any points that St. Thomas spends towards Seamus will be less impactful. The modifier in this case averages to about 0.7833.

### Profile System Feedback

Looking for feedback in terms of how we want to use the profile system. At the moment, I think this would be an entire overhaul of the current system and is designed to be adjusted at the end of every season; whereas RES adjusts every week. The profile system would allow us to granularly rate each team's qualities in a way that we currently cannot with the affinity system. Considering that each player will have preferences towards each quality, we can also guarantee that this may open up recruiting battles in a way so that teams aren’t too focused on participating in the same battles against one another due to affinities.

I am also looking for feedback into how the current math is calculated. If one believes there’s a better way to compare a recruit’s preferences with a team’s values, I am open to it.

Feedback Received

- Playing Time
  - Special dynamic attribute, would need to measure roster size, scheme fit, and players at said position.
- Conference Prestige redux
  - Take the average poll ranking for conferences on a season scale, rank them accordingly.
